title: Traditional Chinese Lunisolar Calendar
intro: Traditional Chinese lunisolar reckoning determines months from the Moon and relates the year to solar seasons.

steps.heading: Watch the changing Moon
steps.text: A lunar month begins around a new moon and usually lasts 29 or 30 days.

steps.heading: Connect the year to the seasons
steps.text: Solar terms help determine the relation of lunar months to the solar year; Chinese New Year moves relative to Gregorian dates.

steps.heading: Understand a leap month
steps.text: Certain years have thirteen months; the extra month is assigned by calendrical rules, not by adding a leap day.

example: A date in a leap-month year needs its year, month, day and leap-month status to identify it unambiguously.
history: Chinese lunisolar dating has long been important for festivals and cultural observances. Its methods and official rules have changed across history.
model: The provider owns year data for 1900–2100, checked against HKO conversion tables for 1901–2100, with 73,048 published dates and one uniquely inferred missing date (2069-12-30). ICU supplies locale text and projection beyond the table. Month navigation counts each intercalary month separately. Year navigation from a leap month absent in the destination year selects the following ordinary month, and day numbers clamp to the target month length. Zero-step navigation preserves the date.
limits: Retrospective results do not certify historical reforms or localities. Future projections beyond the table may differ from official announcements. Modern civic dates generally use Gregorian notation. The date-only representation does not implement a sunset rollover.
